# Missing Data: Diagnosis, Imputation, Reporting {#sec-missing}

```{r}
#| label: missing-hfhome-read
#| include: false
library(dplyr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file, ...) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c", ...,
                                          .default = "?"))
}

hf_rand <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
hf <- hf_rand |>
  select(patient_id, site, arm) |>
  left_join(read_hf("outcomes.csv") |>
              select(patient_id, ascertained, event_30d),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(read_hf("demographics.csv", zip = "c") |>
              select(patient_id, zip),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(
    arm  = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")),
    area = if_else(substr(zip, 1, 3) %in% c("919", "920", "921"),
                   "San Diego area", "Out of state")
  )

stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(hf_rand),
          all(is.na(hf$event_30d) == !hf$ascertained))

by_area <- hf |>
  group_by(area) |>
  summarize(patients = n(), unascertained = sum(!ascertained),
            pct = round(100 * mean(!ascertained), 1))
pct_area <- setNames(by_area$pct, by_area$area)
```

In the HF-HOME trial, `r sum(!hf$ascertained)` of the
`r format(nrow(hf), big.mark = ",")` randomized patients
(`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(!hf$ascertained))`%) have no 30-day
outcome: the health-information exchange that records readmissions
and deaths could not find them. Most had moved away. Among patients
with an out-of-state ZIP code, `r pct_area[["Out of state"]]`% are
unascertained, against `r pct_area[["San Diego area"]]`% of the rest.
R's modeling functions drop those patients without a word, and the
estimate that results is unbiased only if moving away is unrelated
to the outcome, given what the model adjusts for. Nothing in the
data can confirm that, so the real question is not whether the
analysis handles missing values but which assumption it makes about
them, and how far the conclusion moves when that assumption is
wrong.

## Why values go missing {#sec-missing-mechanisms}

Every real clinical dataset has missing values, and the decisions
around them often move an estimate more than the choice of model
does. No method here is free of difficulty. Complete-case analysis
is simple but discards information; multiple imputation keeps it
but adds a model with assumptions of its own; sensitivity analysis
is essential but open-ended. The workable stance is to document the
missingness, state the assumed mechanism and defend it from the
study's conduct, implement one principled approach, and report how
the conclusion moves under the alternatives.

### Three stories

Three patients miss their 30-day assessment, for three different
reasons.

- A case report form (CRF) is lost in the mail. Nothing about the
  patient or the measurement made the loss more likely. This is
  *missing completely at random* ([**MCAR**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mcar-mar-mnar)).
- An older patient misses the visit, as older patients in the trial
  often do. Among patients of the same age, those who miss the visit
  fare no differently from those who attend. Missingness depends
  only on something recorded, so this is *missing at random*
  ([**MAR**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mcar-mar-mnar)).
- A patient whose symptoms worsened stops coming, and the absence is
  itself the bad news. Even among patients alike on everything
  recorded, missingness depends on the value that was not seen. This
  is *missing not at random* ([**MNAR**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mcar-mar-mnar)).

The HF-HOME patients who moved out of state sit in the second story
if moving is unrelated to how they fared; they move to the third if,
say, patients who moved in with family after a bad discharge were
also sicker.

### The definitions

@rubin1976inference made the stories precise. Let $Y$ be the
variable of interest, $R$ the indicator that $Y$ is observed, and
$X$ the other observed variables.

- **MCAR:** $P(R \mid Y, X) = P(R)$. Missingness is independent of
  both observed and unobserved data.
- **MAR:** $P(R \mid Y, X) = P(R \mid X)$. Missingness depends only
  on observed data.
- **MNAR:** $P(R \mid Y, X)$ depends on $Y$ itself, even after
  conditioning on $X$.

The labels describe the missingness process, but they do not by
themselves say which analysis is valid. For the coefficients of a
regression model, the question that decides whether complete-case
analysis is biased is narrower: once the covariates in the model are
held fixed, does missingness still depend on the outcome? If it does
not, complete-case estimates are unbiased whatever the label,
including the MNAR case of a covariate that goes missing because of
its own value. If it does, they are biased, even under MAR
[@white2010bias; @hughes2019accounting]. Multiple imputation and
likelihood methods rest on a different condition, MAR given the
variables in the imputation model. @tbl-missing-mechanisms is
organized by what the missingness depends on.

| Missingness depends on | Label | Complete case | MI / likelihood |
|------------------------|-------|---------------|-----------------|
| Nothing                | MCAR  | Unbiased      | Unbiased        |
| Covariates in the model | MAR  | Unbiased      | Unbiased        |
| Fully observed outcome (covariate missing) | MAR | Biased | Unbiased, outcome in imputation model |
| Auxiliary variable that predicts the outcome | MAR | Biased | Unbiased, auxiliary in imputation model |
| Missing covariate's own value | MNAR | Unbiased | Biased |
| Unobserved outcome, given covariates | MNAR | Biased | Biased |

: Bias of regression coefficients by what missingness depends on.
MI is multiple imputation. The simulation in
@sec-missing-complete-case checks the first, third, and fifth
rows. {#tbl-missing-mechanisms}

Three qualifications. The table concerns regression coefficients: a
mean or prevalence estimated from complete cases is biased under MAR
in general. In logistic regression, missingness that depends on the
outcome alone biases only the intercept, not the odds ratios, by the
argument that justifies case-control designs. And unbiased is not
efficient: a complete-case analysis that is unbiased can still
discard precision that imputation would recover.

@fig-missing-mechanisms draws the three labels as what $R$ depends
on. The arrows say only what the label says; the table above is
what tells you which analysis survives.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-missing-mechanisms
%%| fig-alt: "Three small diagrams side by side, each with nodes X
%%|   (observed covariates), Y (the variable that may be missing),
%%|   and R (whether Y is observed). In MCAR, X points to Y and R
%%|   stands alone. In MAR, X points to Y and to R. In MNAR, X points
%%|   to Y and to R, and Y also points to R."
%%| fig-cap: "The three mechanisms as what the missingness indicator
%%|   R depends on. Under MCAR it depends on nothing; under MAR on
%%|   observed X only; under MNAR on the unseen Y itself. No test on
%%|   the observed data can tell the second diagram from the third."
flowchart LR
  subgraph MCAR
    direction TB
    X1["X"] --> Y1["Y"]
    R1["R"]
  end
  subgraph MAR
    direction TB
    X2["X"] --> Y2["Y"]
    X2 --> R2["R"]
  end
  subgraph MNAR
    direction TB
    X3["X"] --> Y3["Y"]
    X3 --> R3["R"]
    Y3 --> R3
  end
```

### The mechanism is an assumption

MCAR is rare, and MAR is the usual working assumption for a primary
analysis. No row of @tbl-missing-mechanisms can be confirmed from
the observed data, because the data cannot distinguish MAR from
MNAR. 'The patient was lost to follow-up' could be any of the three
stories. The assumption is a substantive claim about why the
missingness occurred, defended by what you know about the data
collection, and a sensitivity analysis under departures from MAR is
expected whatever the primary assumption [@ich2019e9r1].

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft the list of reasons values could be missing,
not to decide which mechanism holds.

> **Context.** Below are a per-variable missingness summary (counts
> and percentages by arm and site) and a paragraph describing how
> the data were collected: who recorded each variable, when, and
> what made a record go missing. No patient-level rows are
> included.
>
> **Constraints.** For each variable, list the plausible reasons
> for missingness and, for each reason, the mechanism it implies
> (MCAR, MAR given named variables, or MNAR). Do not choose a
> single mechanism per variable, and do not propose a statistical
> test that distinguishes MAR from MNAR.
>
> **Criteria.** Every MAR claim names the observed variables it
> conditions on, and those variables appear in my summary. Every
> MNAR reason is paired with the direction of the bias it would
> cause.

*Failure mode.* The model assigns each variable a confident label
and recommends Little's test as confirmation, which can reject MCAR
but can never establish MAR. *Check.* Take the list to the clinical
collaborator; their account of the data collection overrides the
model's guesses, and every MAR claim should map to a variable in
your imputation model. A missingness summary is structure, not
data, so it may go to any approved tool (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks you to justify the assumption that
your data are missing at random. What can you show them, and what
can you not?

**Answer.** You cannot test it. MAR says missingness depends on
*observed* variables; MNAR says it depends on the unobserved values
themselves. The distinguishing evidence is exactly the data you do
not have, so no test on the observed data separates them. A test
that appeared to would be evidence you had the missing values after
all.

What you can show is narrower and still worth showing: that
missingness is *not* MCAR, by demonstrating that it varies with
observed covariates; that every variable predicting missingness is
in the imputation model, which makes MAR plausible rather than
proven; and that the conclusion survives a departure from MAR,
through a delta adjustment or a tipping-point analysis
(@sec-missing-trials). That last one is the real answer to the
reviewer. You do not defend MAR; you show how far from MAR the truth
would have to be before your conclusion changed, and let the reader
judge whether that distance is credible.
:::

## Diagnosing missingness {#sec-missing-diagnosis}

### Looking at the pattern

Before any imputation, look at the pattern. The `naniar` package
provides `ggplot2`-based diagnostics. The row-by-column heatmap
shows at a glance which variables carry missingness and whether it
clusters in particular rows.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vis-miss
#| fig-cap: "Missingness heatmap for the Palmer Penguins data. Each
#|   row is an observation, each column a variable; missing cells are
#|   marked. The `sex` variable carries most of the missingness."
#| fig-alt: "Heatmap of the penguin data with one row per
#|   observation and one column per variable. Present values are
#|   shaded uniformly; missing cells are marked in a contrasting
#|   color. The sex column carries a scattered band of missing
#|   cells; the other columns are nearly solid."
#| fig-scap: "Missingness heatmap for the penguin data"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
library(naniar)
library(palmerpenguins)

vis_miss(penguins)
```

A per-variable bar chart quantifies what the heatmap suggests:

```{r}
#| label: fig-gg-miss-var
#| fig-cap: "Count of missing values per variable. Two body
#|   measurements and `sex` account for essentially all the
#|   missingness in the penguin data."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart counting missing values for each
#|   variable in the penguin data. The bar for sex is much the
#|   longest, two body-measurement variables show short bars, and
#|   the remaining variables have no bar at all."
#| fig-scap: "Count of missing values per variable"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
gg_miss_var(penguins)
```

The UpSet plot shows how missingness co-occurs across variables, and
the case summary counts missing cells per row:

```{r}
#| label: fig-miss-upset
#| fig-cap: "An UpSet plot of missingness intersections in the penguin
#|   data. The bars count rows sharing each combination of missing
#|   variables, which separates rows missing only `sex` from the two
#|   rows missing every morphology measurement."
#| fig-alt: "UpSet plot with a tall bar for rows missing only sex, and
#|   a short bar for the small set of rows missing all four body
#|   measurements together."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| message: false
#| warning: false
gg_miss_upset(penguins)
```

```{r}
#| label: miss-case-summary
miss_case_summary(penguins)
```

Three patterns recur, and each suggests a strategy:

| Pattern | What it looks like | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Univariate | One variable missing, unrelated to the others; often a single CRF page | Any method; check whether it is MCAR |
| Monotone | Once a value is missing, every later one is: visit 5 missing implies visits 6 onward missing, as in longitudinal dropout | Sequential regression imputation, or a likelihood method such as a mixed model |
| Arbitrary | Missing cells scattered across variables and rows; most real clinical data | Chained equations (`mice`) |

: Missingness patterns. {#tbl-missing-patterns}

### Missingness in the running study

In HF-HOME the question is not where the holes are, since only the
outcome has many, but what predicts them. The setup chunk at the top
of this chapter joins randomization, outcomes, and ZIP codes:

```{r}
#| label: missing-hfhome-show
#| ref.label: missing-hfhome-read
#| eval: false
```

Missingness by arm and by area:

```{r}
#| label: missing-hfhome-pattern
hf |>
  group_by(arm, area) |>
  summarize(patients = n(), unascertained = sum(!ascertained),
            pct = round(100 * mean(!ascertained), 1),
            .groups = "drop")
```

Unascertainment is nearly equal in the two arms and is driven by
residence, which is observed. That rules out MCAR in the strict
sense and is consistent with MAR given area. It cannot rule out that
patients who moved fared differently from those who stayed; that is
what the sensitivity analysis in @sec-missing-trials addresses.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A missing-value code read as a number shrinks the missingness and
shifts the mean.** Site D's systems export a missing systolic blood
pressure as `-99`. Read with the default `na = c("", "NA")`, those
cells become measurements: the missingness count drops, the mean
falls, and every downstream model treats `-99` mmHg as a patient.
Declare every code the sources use in `na =` when you read, and
compare the counts against the codebook.
:::

### Exercises

1. `crf_export.csv` holds the same baseline values as
   `baseline.csv`, exported by five site systems with three
   different missing-value conventions. Read its
   `sbp_discharge` column twice, once with the default `na` and
   once declaring every code the README lists. Compare the number
   of missing values and the mean of each version with
   `baseline.csv`.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-17-1
crf_naive <- readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                             col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c"))
crf_coded <- readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                             col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c"),
                             na = c("", "NA", "-99"))
baseline <- read_hf("baseline.csv")

sbp_naive <- as.numeric(crf_naive$sbp_discharge)
sbp_coded <- as.numeric(crf_coded$sbp_discharge)

data.frame(
  source  = c("crf, default na", "crf, codes declared", "baseline"),
  missing = c(sum(is.na(sbp_naive)), sum(is.na(sbp_coded)),
              sum(is.na(baseline$sbp_discharge))),
  mean    = round(c(mean(sbp_naive, na.rm = TRUE),
                    mean(sbp_coded, na.rm = TRUE),
                    mean(baseline$sbp_discharge, na.rm = TRUE)), 1)
)

stopifnot(sum(is.na(sbp_coded)) == sum(is.na(baseline$sbp_discharge)))
```

The default read misses the `-99` cells from Site D, so it reports
fewer missing values and a lower mean than the clean table. Once the
codes are declared, the counts agree with `baseline.csv`. Reading
every column as character first, as here, is what lets you inspect
the codes before anything converts them (Habit 7).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In HF-HOME, unascertainment is about equal in the two
arms. Does that make complete-case analysis of the treatment effect
safe?

**Answer.** No. Equal rates say nothing about *who* is missing in
each arm. If home-health patients who moved were sicker than those
who stayed, while usual-care movers were not, the complete-case
contrast is biased even with identical missingness rates. Balance in
counts is reassuring about power, not about bias; the assumption has
to be argued, and then tested by sensitivity analysis.
:::

## Complete-case analysis {#sec-missing-complete-case}

The simplest approach drops every row with a missing value, and it is
R's default: `lm()`, `glm()`, and most modeling functions use
`na.action = na.omit`.

```{r}
#| label: miss-complete-case
fit_cc <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp, data = airquality)
nrow(fit_cc$model)
nrow(airquality)
```

Complete case is acceptable when missingness does not depend on the
outcome, given the model's covariates; its regression coefficients
are then unbiased whether the mechanism is labeled MCAR, MAR, or
MNAR, though imputation may still gain precision. It is also the
natural sensitivity analysis beside a primary multiple imputation,
because it shows whether the conclusion depends on the imputation
model.

It is not acceptable when missingness plausibly depends on the
outcome, directly or through observed variables outside the analysis
model that predict it. The bias can be large, and the fraction of
rows lost does not by itself bound it: how strongly missingness
depends on the outcome matters as much as how many rows go. No
percentage threshold makes complete case safe.

### Evidence from a simulation

The claims in @tbl-missing-mechanisms are easy to check. The
simulation below deletes about a quarter of a covariate `x` from the
same data-generating model three times, changing only what the
deletion depends on: the other covariate `z`, the outcome `y`, or
`x` itself. Each replicate fits complete case, mean imputation, and
multiple imputation, and records the bias of the coefficient on `x`
and whether the 95% interval covers the truth.

```{r}
#| label: miss-simulation
#| message: false
library(mice)
set.seed(11)

one_rep <- function(depends_on, n = 200, beta = 1) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  z <- rnorm(n)
  y <- beta * x + 0.5 * z + rnorm(n)
  driver <- switch(depends_on, z = z, y = as.vector(scale(y)), x = x)
  x[runif(n) < plogis(-1.6 + 2 * driver)] <- NA
  d <- data.frame(y, x, z)

  d_mean <- d
  d_mean$x[is.na(d_mean$x)] <- mean(d_mean$x, na.rm = TRUE)
  fit_x <- function(data) {
    fit <- lm(y ~ x + z, data = data)
    c(summary(fit)$coefficients["x", 1:2], confint(fit)["x", ])
  }

  # no seed here: a fixed seed would reset the RNG and make
  # every replicate draw the same data
  im <- mice(d, m = 5, printFlag = FALSE)
  s_mi <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(y ~ x + z))), conf.int = TRUE)
  s_mi <- s_mi[s_mi$term == "x", ]

  est <- rbind(cc = fit_x(d), mean = fit_x(d_mean),
               mi = c(s_mi$estimate, s_mi$std.error,
                      s_mi[["2.5 %"]], s_mi[["97.5 %"]]))
  cbind(bias = est[, 1] - beta, se = est[, 2],
        cover = est[, 3] <= beta & beta <= est[, 4])
}

mechanisms <- c("covariate z" = "z", "outcome y" = "y",
                "own value x" = "x")

# 100 replicates rather than 500, to keep the book's build fast
sim <- purrr::map(mechanisms, \(m) {
  reps <- replicate(100, one_rep(m))
  data.frame(method = c("complete case", "mean imputation",
                        "multiple imputation"),
             apply(reps, c(1, 2), mean))
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "depends_on")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-miss-simulation
#| tbl-cap: "Bias of the coefficient on x (true value 1), its average
#|   reported standard error, and coverage of nominal
#|   95% intervals, over 100 replicates per mechanism. Monte Carlo
#|   standard errors are about 0.01 for bias and 0.02 for coverage."
knitr::kable(sim, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Missingness depends on", "Method",
                           "Bias", "SE", "Coverage"))
```

Read the rows before the columns, because the rows are the lesson.
When missingness depends on `z`, a covariate in the model, all three
methods are close to unbiased and cover near 95%. When it depends on
`y`, which is MAR because `y` is fully observed, complete case and
mean imputation are biased and their intervals miss the truth far
more often than 5% of the time, while multiple imputation recovers,
because the outcome is in its imputation model. When `x` goes missing
because of its own value, which is MNAR, complete case is close to
unbiased, because once `x` and `z` are held fixed the deletion does
not depend on `y`, and multiple imputation is the method that is
biased, because it fills the missing values as though they resembled
the observed ones [@white2010bias]. The label did not predict which
method would fail; what the missingness depends on did.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm the three sign changes the table teaches, so that a change
to the simulation that breaks them stops the build:

```{r}
#| label: miss-simulation-verify
bias_of <- function(mech, meth) {
  sim$bias[sim$depends_on == mech & sim$method == meth]
}
stopifnot(
  abs(bias_of("covariate z", "complete case")) < 0.05,
  bias_of("outcome y", "complete case") < -0.05,
  abs(bias_of("outcome y", "multiple imputation")) < 0.05,
  abs(bias_of("own value x", "complete case")) < 0.05,
  bias_of("own value x", "multiple imputation") > 0.03
)
```
:::

### Exercises

2. Add a fourth row: missingness of `x` depends on an auxiliary
   variable `w` that predicts `y` but is not in the analysis model
   `lm(y ~ x + z)`. Predict the bias of complete case, of multiple
   imputation without `w`, and of multiple imputation with `w` in
   the imputation model, then run 100 replicates.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-17-2
set.seed(12)

aux_rep <- function(n = 200, beta = 1) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  z <- rnorm(n)
  y <- beta * x + 0.5 * z + rnorm(n)
  w <- y + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
  x[runif(n) < plogis(-1.6 + 2 * as.vector(scale(w)))] <- NA
  slope <- function(im) {
    s <- summary(pool(with(im, lm(y ~ x + z))))
    s$estimate[s$term == "x"]
  }
  c(cc = coef(lm(y ~ x + z))[["x"]],
    mi_without_w = slope(mice(data.frame(y, x, z), m = 5,
                              printFlag = FALSE)),
    mi_with_w = slope(mice(data.frame(y, x, z, w), m = 5,
                           printFlag = FALSE))) - beta
}

round(rowMeans(replicate(100, aux_rep())), 3)
```

Complete case is biased, because `w` carries information about `y`,
so the deletion depends on the outcome given `x` and `z`. Imputation
without `w` is close to unbiased here only because `y`, which is
nearly `w`, is in the imputation model; with `w` added it does at
least as well. The general rule is the fourth row of
@tbl-missing-mechanisms: include in the imputation model every
variable that predicts missingness and the outcome, even if the
analysis model leaves it out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague drops the 9% of patients with a missing
covariate and says the bias is at most 9% of the effect. Is there
any such bound?

**Answer.** No. The bias depends on how strongly missingness depends
on the outcome given the covariates, not only on how many rows go.
A small fraction deleted by a strong outcome-dependent process can
bias more than a large fraction deleted at random; in the simulation
the 'covariate z' row loses as many rows as the 'outcome y' row and
is unbiased.
:::

## Single imputation, and why it fails {#sec-missing-single}

### Mean imputation

Mean imputation replaces missing values with the sample mean, and it
fails in two ways.

1. The spread of the filled variable is biased downward, because
   the imputed values have no noise. What that does to a standard
   error depends on what was filled: filling an outcome typically
   gives intervals that are too short, while filling a covariate can
   inflate the residual variance and widen them, as the simulation
   shows. Neither error is an honest one.
2. Coefficients can be biased: the filled rows carry no information
   about how the variable relates to the outcome, and when it is
   correlated with other covariates the bias spreads to their
   coefficients too.

```{r}
#| label: miss-antipattern-mean
df <- data.frame(x = c(2, 4, 6, 8, NA, NA))
sd_before <- sd(df$x, na.rm = TRUE)

# do not do this
df$x[is.na(df$x)] <- mean(df$x, na.rm = TRUE)

# the spread has shrunk, and nothing recorded that it did
c(before = sd_before, after = sd(df$x))
```

One setting is an exception. In a randomized trial, a partly missing
*baseline* covariate can be handled by mean imputation or by the
missing-indicator method without biasing the treatment effect,
because randomization makes the covariate independent of the arm
[@white2005adjusting]. Outside that setting, and for the covariate's
own coefficient, both remain antipatterns.

### Carrying values forward, and regression without noise

[**Last observation carried forward (LOCF)**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-locf) assumes that a patient
who drops out stays at the last observed value, which is
biologically implausible for most diseases. The National Research
Council report on missing data in trials recommends against single
imputation methods such as LOCF as the primary approach unless their
assumptions are scientifically justified [@nrc2010prevention], and
Harrell's author checklist [@harrell2024checklist] rules it out
altogether, on the grounds that an assumption no one believes is not
made believable by being labeled a sensitivity analysis.

**Single regression imputation without noise** produces intervals
that are too tight: the imputed values lie exactly on a regression
surface, hiding the variability that should be present.

The common theme is that single imputation pretends the imputed
values have no uncertainty. Multiple imputation fixes this by drawing
many plausible values per missing cell.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the simulation, mean imputation had the *widest*
standard errors, yet the usual warning is that it understates
uncertainty. Which is right?

**Answer.** Both, about different quantities. Mean imputation
shrinks the spread of the variable it fills, which the chunk above
shows directly. But the standard error of a regression coefficient
is not that spread: filling a quarter of a covariate with a constant
destroys the covariance between `x` and `y` in those rows, which
weakens the estimated relationship and inflates the residual
variance, so the reported error goes up. The understatement warning
applies most sharply when the outcome itself is filled in.
:::

## Multiple imputation with mice {#sec-missing-mi}

Multiple imputation proceeds in three steps, shown in @fig-mi-steps:
impute several completed datasets, analyze each one separately, then
pool the results. The fan-out and recombination are the whole point:
the variation between the $M$ analyses carries the uncertainty due
to missingness that single imputation discards.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-mi-steps
%%| fig-alt: "Flowchart of multiple imputation. One incomplete
%%|   dataset fans out into M completed sets, each of which is
%%|   fitted separately. All M fits converge on a pooling node
%%|   applying Rubin's rules, combining within- and between-set
%%|   variance, which yields a single pooled estimate and standard
%%|   error."
%%| fig-cap: "The three steps of multiple imputation. The between-dataset
%%|   variation recovered at the pooling step is the uncertainty that
%%|   single imputation throws away."
flowchart TD
  D["Incomplete<br/>data"] --> S1["Set 1"]
  D --> S2["Set 2"]
  D --> Sm["Set M"]
  S1 --> F1["Fit 1"]
  S2 --> F2["Fit 2"]
  Sm --> Fm["Fit M"]
  F1 --> P["Pool<br/>Rubin's rules<br/><i>within + between variance</i>"]
  F2 --> P
  Fm --> P
  P --> R["One pooled<br/>estimate and SE"]
```

```{r}
#| label: miss-mice
#| message: false
library(mice)

imp <- mice(airquality, m = 25, method = "pmm", seed = 1,
            printFlag = FALSE)
fits <- with(imp, lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp))
pooled <- pool(fits)
summary(pooled, conf.int = TRUE)
```

### Choices in the imputation model

| Argument | Default or choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `method = "pmm"` | Continuous variables | Predictive mean matching draws an observed value from donors whose predictions are closest; robust to misspecification |
| `"logreg"`, `"polyreg"`, `"polr"` | Binary, unordered, ordered categorical | `mice` picks these from the column type |
| `m` | 5 historically; 25 or more now | $M$ should exceed the percentage of missing information [@bodner2008what] |
| `predictorMatrix` | Every other variable, including the outcome | Omitting the outcome biases imputed predictors toward the null [@moons2006using] |
| `seed` | Set once, on the call | Reproducibility; never inside a simulation replicate |

: Choices in a `mice` call. {#tbl-mice-choices}

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Check that `mice` used the methods and predictors you intended:
every incomplete variable has a method, and the outcome predicts
each incomplete covariate.

```{r}
#| label: miss-mice-verify
imp$method
stopifnot(all(imp$method[colSums(is.na(airquality)) > 0] != ""),
          imp$predictorMatrix["Solar.R", "Ozone"] == 1)
```
:::

### Rubin's rules

Pool the $M$ analyses:

- **Pooled point estimate** $\bar\beta = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \hat\beta_m$.
- **Within-imputation variance** $\bar U = \frac{1}{M} \sum_m \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_m)$.
- **Between-imputation variance** $B = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum_m (\hat\beta_m - \bar\beta)^2$.
- **Total variance** $T = \bar U + (1 + 1/M) B$.

The $(1 + 1/M)$ factor is a finite-sample correction. Degrees of
freedom use the Barnard-Rubin adjustment (the `mice` default), which
produces slightly conservative t-tests for moderate $M$.
`mice::pool()` does all of this; inspect the components:

```{r}
#| label: miss-pooled-diagnostics
summary(pooled)$df
summary(pooled)$fmi
summary(pooled)$lambda
```

`fmi`, the fraction of missing information, says how much of the
variance in $\hat\beta$ is due to missing data, and `lambda` the
proportion of total variance attributable to it. Values above 0.5
mean the analysis leans heavily on the imputation model, and
sensitivity analysis matters more.

### Exercises

3. Fit `lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp)` to `airquality` by
   complete-case analysis and by multiple imputation with `m = 20`.
   Compare coefficients and standard errors.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-17-3
#| message: false
cc <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp, data = airquality)

imp20 <- mice(airquality, m = 20, method = "pmm",
              seed = 2, printFlag = FALSE)
mi <- pool(with(imp20, lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp)))

dplyr::bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(cc) |> dplyr::mutate(method = "complete case"),
  summary(mi) |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    dplyr::mutate(method = "multiple imputation")
) |>
  dplyr::select(method, term, estimate, std.error)
```

The coefficients move little; the standard errors are what change,
and they change in both directions. MI uses all 153 rows rather than
the 111 complete ones, which tightens some estimates, while the
between-imputation variance widens others. A method that only ever
tightened intervals would be recovering information it does not
have.
:::

4. Use `mice::ampute()` to induce MAR missingness on the complete
   rows of `airquality`. Fit the model on the full data and on the
   amputed-then-imputed data, and check whether MI recovers the
   full-data coefficients.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-17-4
#| message: false
set.seed(12)
complete_data <- na.omit(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Solar.R",
                                        "Wind", "Temp")])

truth <- coef(lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp,
                 data = complete_data))

amputed <- mice::ampute(complete_data, prop = 0.3,
                        mech = "MAR")$amp
recovered <- summary(pool(with(
  mice(amputed, m = 20, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 3),
  lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp))))

data.frame(term = names(truth),
           truth = round(unname(truth), 3),
           recovered = round(recovered$estimate, 3))
```

MI recovers the full-data coefficients approximately, which is the
claim being checked. 'Approximately' is doing real work: a single run
can miss by more than you expect, and one replicate is a
demonstration rather than evidence. The simulation in
@sec-missing-complete-case is the evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** `mice` with `m = 1` produces a complete dataset in a
fraction of the time. Since the imputation model is the same, what
exactly does the extra work of `m = 20` buy?

**Answer.** Not a better point estimate: one draw and twenty pooled
draws give similar coefficients. What twenty draws buy is the
standard error. Rubin's rules add the *between*-imputation variance,
which measures how much the estimate moves depending on which
plausible values were filled in. A single draw has no between
component, so the reported interval is too narrow. Single
imputation treats a guess as an observation; multiple imputation
makes several guesses and reports how much they disagreed. The
`fmi` above is that disagreement expressed as a fraction, which is
why it cannot be computed from a single imputation.
:::

## Missing outcomes in trials {#sec-missing-trials}

### Start from the estimand

In a trial, what counts as missing depends on the question. A
patient who stopped the study drug and was not followed has missing
data for a *treatment-policy* estimand, which wants the outcome
whatever the patient took; the same unrecorded value is not missing
at all for a *hypothetical* estimand that asks what would have
happened had everyone stayed on treatment. The E9(R1) addendum of
the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) builds the
trial's question around these intercurrent events, and
@sec-analysis-plan-estimands works through them for HF-HOME. Fix the
estimand first; the missing-data method follows from it.

The National Research Council report on missing data in clinical
trials puts prevention before treatment: keep collecting outcomes
after patients stop the assigned treatment, and design and conduct
the trial to limit missing data, because no analysis recovers what
was never measured [@nrc2010prevention]. Its second message is the one this
chapter has been making: state the assumption, and test the
conclusion against departures from it.

### Repeated continuous outcomes: the mixed model

For a continuous outcome measured at several visits, the standard
primary analysis is a mixed model for repeated measures ([**MMRM**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mmrm)):
a likelihood analysis of all observed visits, with arm, visit, their
interaction, and baseline covariates as fixed effects, and an
unstructured covariance across visits. It imputes nothing. Patients
who drop out contribute every visit they attended, and the estimate
at the final visit is valid under MAR given the earlier visits and
covariates, which suits a hypothetical estimand of the effect had
patients continued. The `mmrm` package [@sabanesbove2026mmrm] fits
it; its `fev_data` example has a third of the visits missing:

```{r}
#| label: miss-mmrm
#| message: false
library(mmrm)

fit_mmrm <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ FEV1_BL + RACE + SEX + ARMCD * AVISIT + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = fev_data
)

# treatment effect at the final visit: main effect plus interaction
contrast <- setNames(numeric(length(coef(fit_mmrm))),
                     names(coef(fit_mmrm)))
contrast[c("ARMCDTRT", "ARMCDTRT:AVISITVIS4")] <- 1
df_1d(fit_mmrm, contrast)[c("est", "se", "p_val")]
```

### Reference-based multiple imputation

A treatment-policy estimand asks about patients who stopped the
active treatment, and MAR within arm then assumes they kept
responding like those who stayed on it, which is often implausible.
Reference-based imputation instead borrows the post-discontinuation
trajectory from the reference (control) arm
[@carpenter2013analysis]:

| Method | Assumption after the active-arm patient stops |
|---|---|
| Jump to reference (J2R) | Mean jumps at once to the reference arm's mean |
| Copy reference (CR) | Whole profile, before and after, follows the reference arm's distribution |
| Copy increments in reference (CIR) | Keeps the benefit gained so far; later changes follow the reference arm |

: Reference-based imputation. {#tbl-reference-based}

The `rbmi` package [@gowerpage2022rbmi] implements these with
Bayesian, approximate Bayesian, or conditional-mean imputation. It
is not installed in the environment that builds this book, so the
sketch below is display-only; argument names follow the package
documentation and should be checked against the installed version.

```r
library(rbmi)
vars <- set_vars(subjid = "USUBJID", visit = "AVISIT",
                 outcome = "FEV1", group = "ARMCD",
                 covariates = c("FEV1_BL", "RACE", "SEX",
                                "AVISIT*ARMCD"))
draws_obj <- draws(data = dat, data_ice = dat_ice, vars = vars,
                   method = method_condmean(type = "jackknife"))
imputed <- impute(draws_obj,
                  references = c(PBO = "PBO", TRT = "PBO"))
```

Here `dat_ice` records, per patient, the visit of the intercurrent
event and the strategy (`"JR"` for jump to reference) to apply from
it.

### Delta adjustment and the tipping point

For outcomes without a reference-based model, the usual sensitivity
analysis is a delta adjustment: impute under MAR, shift the imputed
values by $\delta$ to represent patients who fared worse (or better)
than MAR predicts, and refit. In `mice`, pass the shift through the
`post` argument, so that shifted values also inform the imputation
of other variables in later iterations. In a trial, a shift applied
equally to both arms largely cancels in the treatment contrast, so
the informative scenario shifts the active arm only:

```r
post <- make.post(trial)
post["y"] <- paste("idx <- data$arm[where[, j]] == 'active';",
                   "imp[[j]][idx, i] <- imp[[j]][idx, i] +", delta)
imp_delta <- mice(trial, m = 25, post = post, seed = 1,
                  printFlag = FALSE)
```

A [**tipping-point analysis**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-tipping-point-analysis) varies $\delta$ until the conclusion
changes, and asks whether that $\delta$ is clinically plausible.
When each arm gets its own shift, the tipping point becomes a
boundary in two dimensions, $(\delta_{\text{control}},
\delta_{\text{active}})$, and the report shows the region of that
plane in which the conclusion holds [@nrc2010prevention]. Pattern-mixture models
generalize the idea by specifying a separate model per missingness
pattern; delta adjustment is the simplest member of that family.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** HF-HOME is a two-arm randomized trial with a binary
> 30-day outcome; about 7% of outcomes are unascertained, mostly in
> patients with out-of-state addresses. The estimand is attached:
> population, treatment conditions, variable, intercurrent events
> and their strategies, and the risk difference as summary.
>
> **Constraints.** Draft the missing-data section of the
> statistical analysis plan. Name the primary assumption and the
> variables it conditions on, the estimator, and the software. Name
> at least two sensitivity analyses by method (a delta adjustment
> with its scale, grid, and which arms are shifted; a
> two-dimensional tipping point; a reference-based or
> pattern-mixture alternative where it applies). Do not use the
> words 'appropriate' or 'as needed'.
>
> **Criteria.** A second analyst could run every analysis from the
> text alone; each sensitivity analysis departs from a stated
> assumption rather than repeating it; missing patients stay in the
> denominator.

*Failure mode.* The draft says 'sensitivity analyses will be
performed as appropriate', or proposes a delta applied equally to
both arms, which cancels in the contrast. *Check.* For each
sentence, ask 'which?'; if the text does not answer, it is not
pre-specified. Compare the draft with section 11 of the HF-HOME
statistical analysis plan (SAP)
in @sec-analysis-plan-worked.
:::

### Worked example: a two-dimensional tipping point for HF-HOME

HF-HOME's outcome is binary, so the shift is on the risk scale, as
in the SAP (@sec-analysis-plan): unascertained patients in each arm
are assigned $\delta$ times the risk of their observed peers. Each
cell of the grid below is a multiple imputation with $M = 50$. The
arm's risk is drawn from its posterior given the observed patients,
multiplied by that arm's $\delta$, and used to draw outcomes for its
unascertained patients; the risk difference, usual care minus home
health, is pooled by Rubin's rules. The estimator is the unadjusted
difference; the SAP's primary estimator standardizes over baseline
covariates.

```{r}
#| label: miss-hfhome-tipping
set.seed(20260423)

arms <- hf |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(n = n(), n_mis = sum(!ascertained),
            events = sum(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_obs = sum(ascertained), .groups = "drop")

tip_cell <- function(delta_usual, delta_home, m = 50) {
  draws <- replicate(m, {
    p <- rbeta(2, arms$events + 1, arms$n_obs - arms$events + 1)
    p_mis <- pmin(1, p * c(delta_usual, delta_home))
    risk <- (arms$events + rbinom(2, arms$n_mis, p_mis)) / arms$n
    c(est = risk[1] - risk[2], var = sum(risk * (1 - risk) / arms$n))
  })
  q_bar <- mean(draws["est", ])
  b <- var(draws["est", ])
  t_var <- mean(draws["var", ]) + (1 + 1 / m) * b
  df <- (m - 1) * (1 + mean(draws["var", ]) / ((1 + 1 / m) * b))^2
  half <- qt(0.975, df) * sqrt(t_var)
  100 * c(estimate = q_bar, lower = q_bar - half, upper = q_bar + half)
}

grid <- expand.grid(delta_usual = seq(0.5, 2, by = 0.25),
                    delta_home  = seq(0.5, 2, by = 0.25))
grid <- cbind(grid, t(mapply(tip_cell, grid$delta_usual,
                             grid$delta_home)))
grid$conclusion <- with(grid, ifelse(lower > 0, "Benefit",
                                     ifelse(upper < 0, "Harm",
                                            "Inconclusive")))

grid |> filter(delta_usual == 1, delta_home == 1)
table(grid$conclusion)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-miss-tipping
#| fig-cap: "Two-dimensional tipping point for HF-HOME. Each cell is
#|   the pooled risk difference (usual care minus home health, in
#|   percentage points) when unascertained patients in each arm have
#|   delta times the risk of their observed peers. Outlined cells are
#|   those whose 95% interval excludes zero; the cell at (1, 1) is
#|   MAR."
#| fig-alt: "Seven-by-seven grid of tiles, delta for usual care on the
#|   horizontal axis and delta for home health on the vertical axis,
#|   both from 0.5 to 2. Each tile shows the risk difference; values
#|   are largest at the bottom right, where usual-care missing
#|   patients are assumed to do worse and home-health missing
#|   patients better. Outlined tiles, where the interval excludes
#|   zero, lie in that bottom-right region; the rest of the grid,
#|   including the center, is inconclusive."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(grid, aes(delta_usual, delta_home, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_tile(aes(color = conclusion != "Inconclusive"),
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", estimate)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(midpoint = 0, low = "#b2182b",
                       high = "#2166ac", mid = "white",
                       name = "Risk\ndifference") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = NA, `TRUE` = "black"),
                     guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Delta, usual care", y = "Delta, home health") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Under MAR (the cell at 1, 1) the result is inconclusive, as it is in
the complete-case analysis. The grid shows which departures would
change that. `r sum(grid$conclusion == "Benefit")` of the
`r nrow(grid)` cells conclude benefit, and in every one of them
$\delta$ is larger for usual care than for home health: unascertained
usual-care patients fared worse than their observed peers, relative
to unascertained home-health patients. The number of cells that
conclude harm is `r sum(grid$conclusion == "Harm")`. Whether the
benefit region is
plausible is a clinical question, and the report has to answer it in
words: is there any reason to think that patients who moved away did
worse on usual care than on home health?

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The MAR cell should reproduce the complete-case risk difference,
because with $\delta = 1$ in both arms the imputation adds noise but
no shift, and every benefit cell should lie where usual care's
$\delta$ exceeds home health's, as the text says:

```{r}
#| label: miss-tipping-verify
cc_rd <- 100 * with(arms, events[1] / n_obs[1] - events[2] / n_obs[2])
mar_rd <- grid$estimate[grid$delta_usual == 1 & grid$delta_home == 1]
round(c(complete_case = cc_rd, mar_cell = mar_rd), 2)
stopifnot(abs(cc_rd - mar_rd) < 0.5,
          with(grid[grid$conclusion == "Benefit", ],
               all(delta_usual > delta_home)))
```
:::

The missing-data plan, including the primary assumption, $M$, the
imputation methods, and every sensitivity analysis with its range of
$\delta$, belongs in the statistical analysis plan, written and
tagged before the outcome data are seen; @sec-analysis-plan covers
how.

### Exercises

5. Implement a delta-adjustment sensitivity analysis for a
   multiple-imputation logistic regression with a partly missing
   covariate. Vary $\delta$ over $(-1, 1)$ in steps of 0.25, plot
   the coefficient against $\delta$, and identify the tipping point
   if any.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: fig-soln-17-4
#| fig-cap: "A delta-adjustment sensitivity curve. The coefficient is
#|   plotted against the shift applied to imputed values; the
#|   horizontal line marks zero. Where the curve crosses it, if it
#|   does, is the tipping point."
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a logistic-regression coefficient against
#|   delta from -1 to 1. The curve is nearly flat at first, then
#|   declines as delta increases, with a dashed horizontal reference
#|   line at zero."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| message: false
set.seed(13)
n <- 400
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n))
d$y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.4 * d$x))
d$x[runif(n) < 0.25] <- NA

delta_fit <- function(delta) {
  post <- make.post(d)
  post["x"] <- paste("imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] +", delta)
  im <- mice(d, m = 10, post = post, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 4)
  s <- summary(pool(with(im, glm(y ~ x, family = binomial))))
  s$estimate[s$term == "x"]
}

deltas <- seq(-1, 1, by = 0.25)
curve <- data.frame(delta = deltas,
                    estimate = vapply(deltas, delta_fit, numeric(1)))

ggplot2::ggplot(curve, ggplot2::aes(delta, estimate)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2)
```

The coefficient moves smoothly with $\delta$, so the question is
whether it crosses zero inside a range of $\delta$ you consider
plausible. If it does not, the conclusion is robust to this
departure from MAR; if it does, the crossing point is what the
report should quote, alongside an argument about which values of
$\delta$ are credible.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A common one-directional tipping-point rule increases
$\delta$ in the active arm 'until the 95% interval includes zero'.
What would that rule report for this draw of the HF-HOME data, and
why does the HF-HOME analysis plan (@sec-analysis-plan) use the
two-dimensional grid instead?

**Answer.** Nothing useful: the interval already includes zero at
$\delta = 1$, so there is nothing to tip. A one-directional rule
quietly assumes the primary result will be positive. The
two-dimensional grid answers the question for any result, which is
why the plan pre-specifies it: it shows which departures would
change the conclusion in either direction.
:::

## Going further {#sec-missing-further}

### Values below a limit of detection

An assay that reports a concentration only above its limit of
detection returns, below it, not a value but the information that
the value is small. This is *left censoring*, not missingness, and
an analysis that discards those observations or substitutes a
constant such as the limit divided by $\sqrt{2}$ distorts the
variance in ways multiple imputation under MAR will not repair. The
methods that suit it are regression on order statistics, censored
maximum likelihood, and multiple imputation adapted to the
threshold.[^lod] Before choosing a missing-data method, establish
whether the values are missing or merely unobserved below a bound.

[^lod]: The in-house `zzmesoimpute` package provides a common
    interface across these methods for multiplexed immunoassay data,
    the setting where the problem is most often met.

### Reporting standards

The reporting guidelines, CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of
Reporting Trials) for randomized trials and STROBE (Strengthening the
Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) for
observational studies, set the floor for what a paper says about
missing data:

| Guideline | Item | What to report |
|---|---|---|
| CONSORT 2010 [@schulz2010consort] | 13b | Losses and exclusions after randomization in each arm, with reasons |
| CONSORT 2010 | 16 | Number analyzed in each arm, and whether by original assignment |
| STROBE [@vonelm2007strobe] | 12c | How missing data were addressed |
| STROBE | 14b | Number of participants with missing data for each variable of interest |

: Missing-data items in the reporting guidelines, as of
2026-10.[^consort] {#tbl-missing-reporting}

[^consort]: CONSORT was revised in 2025, and the revision renumbers
    its items; check the version the journal requires before citing
    an item number.

Harrell's author checklist [@harrell2024checklist] adds an item the
guidelines leave implicit: an incomplete record is not a disposable
one. Dropping every patient with any missing covariate needs the
same justification in the methods section as an imputation model
would. If the complete-case sample differs from the enrolled sample
in ways the reader can check, show the comparison; if it does not
differ on anything you measured, say so, and say what you could not
measure.

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** Dropped rows and filled-in means produce clean
   output; state the mechanism you assume and what it depends on.
2. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** Choose the primary approach,
   $M$, and the sensitivity analyses before the outcomes are seen,
   or the choice becomes another researcher degree of freedom.
3. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** A completed
   dataset with no `NA` passes every structural check; check the
   imputation model, include the outcome in it, and show how far the
   conclusion moves under departures from MAR.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins and @sec-analysis-plan).* Build the
   HF-HOME analysis dataset from `randomization.csv`,
   `outcomes.csv`, and `baseline.csv`, declaring each join's
   relationship. Report the CONSORT 13b counts by arm, fit the
   complete-case logistic regression of the SAP's primary model,
   and write a methods paragraph on missing data that states the
   assumption, the estimator, and the sensitivity analysis, with
   every number computed inline.
7. *On your own work (no key).* For an analysis you have completed,
   find every place rows were dropped for missing values, including
   the silent drops in model fits. State what the missingness in
   each depends on, and whether the complete-case estimates are
   defensible under @tbl-missing-mechanisms.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code or rule | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| See the pattern | `naniar::vis_miss(d)`, `gg_miss_upset(d)` | Imputing before looking |
| Declare missing codes | `read_csv(f, na = c("", "NA", "-99"))` | Codes read as values |
| Count rows a model used | `nrow(fit$model)` | Silent complete-case drops |
| Decide on complete case | Does missingness depend on the outcome, given the covariates? | Trusting the MCAR/MAR/MNAR label |
| Impute | `mice(d, m = 25, seed = 1)` | Too few imputations |
| Check the imputation model | `imp$method`, `imp$predictorMatrix` | Outcome left out |
| Pool | `pool(with(imp, lm(...)))` | Single-imputation intervals |
| Repeated continuous outcome | `mmrm(y ~ ... + us(visit \| id))` | Discarding dropouts' earlier visits |
| Shift imputed values | `post` argument of `mice()`, active arm only | A delta that cancels in the contrast |
| Sensitivity | Two-dimensional tipping point | A one-directional rule with nothing to tip |

## Further reading

- [@vanbuuren2018flexible], *Flexible Imputation of Missing Data*,
  2nd ed., the book-length treatment of the `mice` approach.
- [@little2019statistical], *Statistical Analysis with Missing
  Data*, 3rd ed., the authoritative reference.
- [@nrc2010prevention], the National Research Council report on
  preventing and treating missing data in clinical trials.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-17}

1. **MCAR** (Missing Completely At Random): the probability of
   missingness is independent of both observed and unobserved data.
   Complete-case analysis is unbiased but inefficient. **MAR**
   (Missing At Random): missingness depends only on *observed* data;
   conditional on the observed, it is independent of the unobserved.
   Model-based methods (multiple imputation, likelihood) are
   consistent. **MNAR** (Missing Not At Random): missingness depends
   on the unobserved data itself. No method is consistent in general
   without additional assumptions. For regression coefficients, the
   label does not settle whether complete-case analysis is biased:
   it is unbiased whenever missingness does not depend on the
   outcome given the model's covariates, which can hold under MAR or
   MNAR, and biased when it does, which can happen under MAR.
   Because MAR cannot be tested against MNAR, sensitivity analysis
   is expected under any primary assumption.
2. [**Complete-case analysis**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-complete-case-analysis) drops the ~12% of rows with missing
   data, reducing the effective sample size; its coefficient
   estimates are unbiased if missingness does not depend on the
   outcome given the covariates, whatever the mechanism label, and
   biased if it does. [**Mean imputation**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-mean-imputation) replaces missing values
   with the sample mean. It understates the spread of the filled
   variable and can bias coefficients, but its standard errors are
   not reliably too narrow: for a missing predictor the filled rows
   inflate the residual variance, and the simulation in this chapter
   shows its standard error is the widest of the three methods. It
   is wrong in either direction, except for a baseline covariate in
   a randomized trial, where it leaves the treatment effect
   unbiased. [**Multiple imputation**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-multiple-imputation) produces $M$ plausible
   completed datasets, fits the model on each, and pools with
   Rubin's rules; the pooled standard error correctly reflects both
   within- and between-imputation uncertainty.
3. Rubin's rules combine (i) the mean of the $M$ point estimates,
   (ii) the mean of the $M$ within-imputation variances (the within
   component), and (iii) the variance of the $M$ point estimates
   scaled by $(1 + 1/M)$ (the between component). The pooled
   variance is within + between; the pooled estimate is the mean of
   estimates; degrees of freedom use the Barnard-Rubin adjustment.
